chapter.title: Getting started with Python
chapter.html:
What is Python and why learn it?

Python is a general-purpose programming language, which means it can be used to build many different kinds of software rather than being limited to one narrow task. It was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. One of Python’s main design goals is readability: Python code is meant to look close to plain English compared with many other programming languages.

A programming language lets you give precise instructions to a computer. Python is especially popular because it works well for beginners while also being powerful enough for professional projects. It is used in web development, data science, automation, education, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, game scripting, and scientific computing.

Where Python is used in real work

Python often appears in situations where people need to process information, automate repeated actions, or build software quickly. For example, a small business might use Python to rename hundreds of invoice files, extract totals from spreadsheets, or send automatic email reminders. A data analyst might use Python to clean survey results and create charts. A web developer might use Python to build the server side of a website, such as handling user accounts or storing form submissions.

Domain Example use Why Python fits
Automation Rename files, organize folders, generate reports Python can interact with files, dates, text, and operating system tools
Data science Analyze sales, survey, or experiment data Python has strong libraries for tables, statistics, and visualization
Web development Create websites and web APIs Python frameworks help developers build reliable server-side applications
Education Learn programming fundamentals Python syntax is readable and beginner-friendly

Why Python is beginner-friendly

Python is not “easy” because computers are easy; programming still requires careful thinking. Python is beginner-friendly because it removes some unnecessary complexity from the first learning experience. Its syntax is relatively clean, and common operations can often be written in a small number of lines.

For example, this Python program displays a message:

print("Hello, Python!")

The instruction print() tells Python to display output. The text inside quotation marks is a string, which means a piece of text data. You do not need to understand every detail yet. For now, notice that the code is readable: it looks like a direct instruction.

Less effective and more effective ways to start

A less effective approach is to begin by memorizing many commands without understanding what they do. This can make programming feel like copying magic phrases. A more effective approach is to connect each line of code to a simple question: What instruction am I giving? What information does it use? What result should I expect?

Less effective approach More effective approach
Copying code without running it Running code and observing the exact output
Trying to learn every Python feature at once Learning a small concept, then testing it with examples
Ignoring error messages Reading error messages as clues about what Python could not understand
Typing large programs immediately Starting with short programs that are easy to inspect

Setting up Python

To run Python programs, your computer needs a Python interpreter. An interpreter is a program that reads your Python code and carries out the instructions. You can install Python from the official Python website at https://www.python.org/downloads/.

Windows

  1. Download the latest stable Python installer from the official website.
  2. Run the installer.
  3. On the first installer screen, select Add python.exe to PATH if the option appears.
  4. Choose the standard installation option.
  5. Open Command Prompt or PowerShell and verify the installation.
py --version

macOS

  1. Download the macOS installer from the official Python website, or use a trusted package manager if you already know one.
  2. Run the installer and follow the prompts.
  3. Open Terminal and verify the installation.
python3 --version

Linux

Many Linux systems already include Python. Open a terminal and check the installed version:

python3 --version

If Python is not installed, use your distribution’s package manager. For example, on Debian-based systems such as Ubuntu, you may use:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3

Common setup pitfalls

  • Using the wrong command: On Windows, py often works. On macOS and Linux, python3 is commonly used.
  • Forgetting PATH on Windows: If the command is not recognized, Python may be installed but not available from the command line.
  • Installing from an unofficial source: Prefer the official Python website or your operating system’s trusted package manager.
  • Confusing Python with a code editor: Python runs code. A code editor helps you write code. They are related, but not the same thing.

Short activity: connect Python to a real task

Choose one repeated computer task from your daily life, schoolwork, or job. Write one or two sentences describing how Python might help. For example: “I often download files with messy names. Python could rename them using a consistent date and category format.” Then verify your Python installation by running the version command for your operating system.

Writing your first Python program

There are two common ways to begin using Python: the interactive shell and script files. The interactive shell is useful for quick experiments because you type one instruction and see the result immediately. A script file is better for saving a program so you can run it again later.

Using the interactive shell

Open a terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell. Start Python with the command that matches your system. On Windows, this is often:

py

On macOS or Linux, this is often:

python3

When the Python prompt appears, it usually looks like this:

>>>

You can use the shell like a calculator:

>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> 10 * 4
40
>>> print("Python is running")
Python is running

The shell is useful because it gives immediate feedback. If you are unsure what a small expression does, you can test it quickly. To leave the shell, you can usually type exit() and press Enter.

>>> exit()

Creating a script file

A script is a saved file containing Python instructions. Create a new file in a plain-text code editor and name it hello.py. The .py extension tells you and your tools that the file contains Python code.

Type this code into the file:

print("Hello, Python!")
print("This is my first script.")

Save the file. Then open a terminal in the same folder as the file and run it. On Windows, use:

py hello.py

On macOS or Linux, use:

python3 hello.py

You should see:

Hello, Python!
This is my first script.

Understanding input, processing, and output

A program can be understood as a sequence that receives or uses information, processes it, and produces a result. This is often described as input, processing, output.

  • Input: The information a program starts with. This might come from a user, a file, a sensor, a website, or values written in the program.
  • Processing: The steps the program performs, such as calculating, comparing, organizing, or formatting information.
  • Output: The result the program produces, such as printed text, a saved file, a chart, or an action.

In the first script, the input is the text written inside the code, the processing is Python carrying out the print() instructions, and the output is the displayed text.

Here is a slightly more realistic example from a small shop preparing a receipt message:

print("Receipt")
print("Item: notebook")
print("Price: $4.50")
print("Thank you for your purchase!")

This is still simple, but it already shows a useful pattern: a program can turn stored information into clear output. Later, programs can become more flexible by using information that changes, but the basic structure remains the same: information goes in, instructions are applied, and a result comes out.

Ineffective and effective first programs

A less effective first program tries to do too many things at once: calculations, user interaction, file saving, and complex formatting all in one attempt. When an error occurs, it becomes difficult to know which part caused the problem. A more effective first program has a narrow purpose and produces visible output, making it easier to test and understand.

Less effective first attempt More effective first attempt
A long program copied from the internet A short program you type, run, and modify yourself
No clear expected output A clear prediction of what should appear on screen
Changing many lines before testing Changing one line, running the program, and observing the result

Common mistakes when running a first script

  • Missing quotation marks: Text must be placed inside quotation marks, such as "Hello".
  • Using curved quotes: Code editors should use straight quotes ", not word processor quotes like “ and ”.
  • Saving with the wrong file extension: A file named hello.py.txt may not run as expected. The filename should end in .py.
  • Running the command from the wrong folder: The terminal must be in the folder where hello.py is saved, unless you provide the full path.
  • Typing commands inside the wrong place: Operating system commands like python3 hello.py go in the terminal, not inside the Python script itself.

Short activity: modify and predict

  1. Create a file named first_message.py.
  2. Add three print() lines that display your name, one reason you are learning Python, and one task you think a program could help with.
  3. Before running the file, write down exactly what you expect to appear.
  4. Run the file and compare the actual output with your prediction.
  5. Change one line, run the file again, and observe how the output changes.

If the program does not run, treat the error message as information rather than failure. Check the filename, command, folder location, spelling of print, parentheses, and quotation marks.

This chapter introduced Python as a readable, versatile programming language, showed how to install and verify the interpreter, and demonstrated two ways to run Python code: quick experiments in the interactive shell and saved instructions in a script file. It also explained programs through the pattern of input, processing, and output, using simple printed messages as the first working examples.

Writing your first Python program

There are two common ways to begin using Python: the interactive shell and script files. The interactive shell is useful for quick experiments because you type one instruction and see the result immediately. A script file is better for saving a program so you can run it again later.
Using the interactive shell
Open a terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell. Start Python with the command that matches your system. On Windows, this is often:
py
On macOS or Linux, this is often:
python3
When the Python prompt appears, it usually looks like this:
>>>
You can use the shell like a calculator:

>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> 10 * 4
40
>>> print("Python is running")
Python is running
The shell is useful because it gives immediate feedback. If you are unsure what a small expression does, you can test it quickly. To leave the shell, you can usually type exit() and press Enter.
>>> exit()
Creating a script file

A script is a saved file containing Python instructions. Create a new file in a plain-text code editor and name it hello.py. The .py extension tells you and your tools that the file contains Python code.
Type this code into the file:

print("Hello, Python!")
print("This is my first script.")
Save the file. Then open a terminal in the same folder as the file and run it. On Windows, use:
py hello.py
On macOS or Linux, use:
python3 hello.py
You should see:

Hello, Python!
This is my first script.
Understanding input, processing, and output
A program can be understood as a sequence that receives or uses information, processes it, and produces a result. This is often described as input, processing, output.

• Input: The information a program starts with. This might come from a user, a file, a sensor, a website, or values written in the program.
  • Processing: The steps the program performs, such as calculating, comparing, organizing, or formatting information.
  • Output: The result the program produces, such as printed text, a saved file, a chart, or an action.
In the first script, the input is the text written inside the code, the processing is Python carrying out the print() instructions, and the output is the displayed text.
Here is a slightly more realistic example from a small shop preparing a receipt message:

print("Receipt")
print("Item: notebook")
print("Price: $4.50")
print("Thank you for your purchase!")

This is still simple, but it already shows a useful pattern: a program can turn stored information into clear output. Later, programs can become more flexible by using information that changes, but the basic structure remains the same: information goes in, instructions are applied, and a result comes out.
Ineffective and effective first programs

A less effective first program tries to do too many things at once: calculations, user interaction, file saving, and complex formatting all in one attempt. When an error occurs, it becomes difficult to know which part caused the problem. A more effective first program has a narrow purpose and produces visible output, making it easier to test and understand.

Less effective first attempt More effective first attempt
A long program copied from the internet A short program you type, run, and modify yourself
No clear expected output A clear prediction of what should appear on screen
Changing many lines before testing Changing one line, running the program, and observing the result
Common mistakes when running a first script

• Missing quotation marks: Text must be placed inside quotation marks, such as "Hello".
  • Using curved quotes: Code editors should use straight quotes ", not word processor quotes like “ and ”.
  • Saving with the wrong file extension: A file named hello.py.txt may not run as expected. The filename should end in .py.
  • Running the command from the wrong folder: The terminal must be in the folder where hello.py is saved, unless you provide the full path.
  • Typing commands inside the wrong place: Operating system commands like python3 hello.py go in the terminal, not inside the Python script itself.
Short activity: modify and predict

1. Create a file named first_message.py.
  2. Add three print() lines that display your name, one reason you are learning Python, and one task you think a program could help with.
  3. Before running the file, write down exactly what you expect to appear.
  4. Run the file and compare the actual output with your prediction.
  5. Change one line, run the file again, and observe how the output changes.
If the program does not run, treat the error message as information rather than failure. Check the filename, command, folder location, spelling of print, parentheses, and quotation marks.

It also explained programs through the pattern of input, processing, and output, using simple printed messages as the first working examples.

chapter.title: Variables and data types
chapter.html:
Storing data with variables

In your first Python programs, you printed fixed messages. Variables let a program remember information while it runs, so the program can process values instead of only displaying text that never changes. A variable is a name that refers to a value. You create one with an assignment statement, using the equals sign =.

student_name = "Maya"
lesson_count = 2
print(student_name)
print(lesson_count)

Read student_name = "Maya" as “store the value "Maya" using the name student_name.” It is not the same as mathematical equality. In Python, the right side is evaluated first, and then the result is assigned to the name on the left.

Choosing names that make code readable

Variable names can contain letters, numbers, and underscores, but they cannot start with a number. Python is also case-sensitive, so score, Score, and SCORE are three different names. For beginner-friendly code, prefer clear lowercase names with underscores between words.

Variable name Valid? Reason
total_price Yes Clear, lowercase, and uses an underscore.
2nd_place No Names cannot begin with a number.
studentName Yes Valid, though student_name is more common in Python.
class No class is a reserved Python keyword.

Reassigning values

A variable can be assigned a new value later. This is useful when a program tracks a changing quantity, such as points in a game, items in a shopping cart, or the current temperature reading from a sensor.

score = 0
print(score)
score = 10
print(score)
score = score + 5
print(score)

The line score = score + 5 means: take the current value of score, add 5, and store the result back into score. This pattern is common because programs often update stored data during processing.

A realistic example: tracking a small order

Imagine a small bakery script that calculates the cost of a customer’s order before printing a receipt message. Variables make the program easier to understand because each important piece of information has a meaningful name.

item_name = "blueberry muffin"
quantity = 3
price_each = 2.50
subtotal = quantity * price_each
print("Item:")
print(item_name)
print("Subtotal:")
print(subtotal)

This example separates the data from the calculation. If the customer buys 4 muffins instead of 3, you only need to update quantity. If the price changes, you only need to update price_each. The calculation stays readable.

Ineffective and effective variable use

An ineffective approach often repeats literal values or uses vague names. This makes the code harder to check and easier to break when values change.

x = 3
y = 2.50
print(x * y)

This works, but the meaning of x and y is not obvious. A more effective version names the data according to its role.

quantity = 3
price_each = 2.50
subtotal = quantity * price_each
print(subtotal)

The effective version is not longer by accident; it is clearer by design. Good variable names reduce the amount of guessing needed when reading code.

Common pitfalls with variables

  • Using a variable before assigning it, such as print(total) before total has been created.
  • Accidentally changing capitalization, such as assigning user_name but printing User_name.
  • Choosing names that hide meaning, such as a, b, and c for important values.
  • Confusing assignment with equality; = stores a value in a name.

Practice: describe the data before coding

Write a short program for a movie ticket purchase. Create variables for the movie title, number of tickets, ticket price, and total cost. Print each important value. Before running it, ask yourself: “If someone else read only my variable names, would they understand what the program is storing?”

Working with numbers and strings

Values in Python have data types. A data type tells Python what kind of value it is working with and what operations make sense. Two of the most common categories are numbers and strings. Numbers are used for arithmetic, measurements, counts, and prices. Strings are used for text, labels, names, messages, and any sequence of characters.

Integers, floats, and arithmetic

An integer, or int, is a whole number such as 8, 0, or -15. A floating-point number, or float, includes a decimal point, such as 3.14 or 2.50. Python supports common arithmetic operators.

Operator Meaning Example
+ Addition 8 + 2
- Subtraction 8 - 2
* Multiplication 8 * 2
/ Division 8 / 2
// Floor division 9 // 2
% Remainder 9 % 2
** Power 2 ** 3 
hours_worked = 6
hourly_rate = 15.50
daily_pay = hours_worked * hourly_rate
print(daily_pay)

When an arithmetic expression combines an int and a float, the result is usually a float. That is why money, measurements, and averages often involve decimal values.

Strings as stored text

A string, or str, is text enclosed in quotation marks. You can use single quotes or double quotes, as long as the opening and closing marks match.

first_name = "Ari"
last_name = "Chen"
full_name = first_name + " " + last_name
print(full_name)

With strings, + means concatenation, which joins text together. The space in " " is also a string, and it matters because Python does not add spaces automatically.

Strings can also be repeated with *.

divider = "-" * 20
print(divider)
print("Receipt")
print(divider)

String indexing

Each character in a string has a position called an index. Python starts counting at 0, not 1. This is important because many Python tools use zero-based indexing.

word = "Python"
print(word[0])
print(word[1])
print(word[5])

In this example, word[0] is "P", and word[5] is "n". If you try an index that is outside the string, Python raises an error because there is no character at that position.

Converting between types

Python does not automatically guess every conversion you want. If a number is stored as text, arithmetic will not work until you convert it. The most common conversion functions are int(), float(), and str().

ticket_count_text = "4"
ticket_price_text = "12.50"
ticket_count = int(ticket_count_text)
ticket_price = float(ticket_price_text)
total = ticket_count * ticket_price
print("Total cost: " + str(total))

The final line uses str(total) because concatenation joins strings, not a string and a number directly.

Ineffective and effective type handling

An ineffective approach treats text that looks like a number as if it already were a number.

quantity = "3"
price_each = "2.50"
total = quantity * price_each

This fails because multiplying two strings is not meaningful in Python. A better approach converts the values before calculating.

quantity = int("3")
price_each = float("2.50")
total = quantity * price_each
print(total)

The effective version makes the type change explicit. This makes the program’s processing step more reliable and easier to inspect.

Common pitfalls with numbers and strings

  • Writing "10" + "5" and expecting 15; the result is the string "105".
  • Trying to concatenate text and a number without converting the number using str().
  • Forgetting that string indexes start at 0.
  • Using int() on decimal text such as "12.50"; use float() for decimal values.
  • Assuming / keeps whole numbers; division with / produces a float.

Practice: fix the receipt calculation

Study the program below, then rewrite it so it calculates the total correctly and prints a readable message.

item = "notebook"
quantity = "5"
price = "3.25"
total = quantity * price
print("Total for " + quantity + " " + item + ": " + total)

After fixing it, test your version with a different quantity and price. Notice which values should remain strings and which values should be converted for arithmetic.

This chapter showed how variables store values, how clear names make code easier to understand, how reassignment updates stored data, and how Python works with common data types such as integers, floats, and strings. It also covered arithmetic, string concatenation and repetition, indexing, and explicit type conversion with int(), float(), and str().

chapter.title: Making decisions with conditionals
chapter.html:
Using if statements to make choices

Programs become more useful when they can choose between different actions. An if statement tells Python to run a block of code only when a condition is true. A condition is an expression that produces either True or False, often by comparing values stored in variables.

temperature = 32
if temperature >= 30:
    print("It is a hot day.")

The line ending with a colon starts the decision. The indented line below it belongs to the if block. Python uses indentation to understand which statements are controlled by the decision.

How comparisons create decisions

Comparison operators let your program ask precise questions about values. The result of each comparison is a Boolean value: True or False.

Operator Meaning Example Result if score = 80
== Equal to score == 80 True
!= Not equal to score != 80 False
< Less than score < 80 False
> Greater than score > 80 False
<= Less than or equal to score <= 80 True
>= Greater than or equal to score >= 80 True

A common beginner mistake is confusing = and ==. A single = assigns a value to a variable. A double == compares two values.

score = 80      # assignment
score == 80     # comparison

Adding alternatives with else and elif

An if statement handles one possible path. An else block handles the opposite case. This is useful when a program must choose between two outcomes.

account_balance = 45
purchase_total = 30
if account_balance >= purchase_total:
    print("Purchase approved.")
else:
    print("Not enough funds.")

For more than two possibilities, use elif, which means “else if.” Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is true. After that, the rest of the chain is skipped.

score = 86
if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
else:
    grade = "Needs improvement"
print(grade)

The order matters. In the example above, score >= 80 must come before score >= 70. If broader conditions are placed too early, more specific conditions may never run.

A realistic decision: choosing a shipping message

Online stores often show different messages depending on the value of an order. The program below uses a variable and several conditions to choose a helpful message.

order_total = 72.50
if order_total >= 100:
    message = "You qualify for free express shipping."
elif order_total >= 50:
    message = "You qualify for free standard shipping."
else:
    message = "Shipping costs will be added at checkout."
print(message)

This is more flexible than writing separate one-off print statements because the program chooses the message based on the current value of order_total. If the value changes, the decision changes with it.

Ineffective and effective condition chains

Ineffective approach Why it causes problems Effective approach
if score >= 70
elif score >= 90		 The 90 case is never reached because scores of 90 or higher already match score >= 70. Check the most specific or highest range first: if score >= 90, then elif score >= 70.
Using several separate if statements for one exclusive choice More than one block might run when only one result should be selected. Use an if, elif, else chain when the choices are mutually exclusive.
Writing vague conditions such as if total before understanding the intended test The code may technically run but be hard to read or reason about. Write explicit comparisons such as if total >= 50 when checking a threshold.

Common mistakes with basic conditionals

  • Using = instead of == when comparing values.
  • Forgetting the colon after if, elif, or else.
  • Indenting inconsistently, which changes which lines belong to the conditional block.
  • Putting conditions in an order that makes later cases unreachable.
  • Using separate if statements when only one branch should run.

Activity: classify an account balance

Create a variable named balance and write a conditional chain that prints one of three messages:

  • "Overdrawn" if the balance is less than 0.
  • "Low balance" if the balance is from 0 up to, but not including, 100.
  • "Balance is healthy" if the balance is 100 or more.

Test your code with at least three different values, such as -15, 50, and 200. After each test, check whether the output matches the condition you intended.

Combining conditions with logical operators

Many real decisions depend on more than one condition. Python provides logical operators that combine Boolean expressions: and, or, and not. These operators help you express rules such as “the user must be old enough and have permission” or “apply a discount if the customer is a member or has a coupon.”

Using and when all conditions must be true

The and operator produces True only when both sides are true.

age = 20
has_ticket = True
if age >= 18 and has_ticket == True:
    print("Entry allowed.")
else:
    print("Entry denied.")

This condition requires both rules to pass: the person must be at least 18 and must have a ticket. If either part is false, the entire condition is false.

Because has_ticket already stores a Boolean value, the comparison can be written more directly:

age = 20
has_ticket = True
if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Entry allowed.")
else:
    print("Entry denied.")

Using or when at least one condition may be true

The or operator produces True when at least one side is true. This is useful for alternative ways to qualify for the same outcome.

is_member = False
has_coupon = True
if is_member or has_coupon:
    print("Discount applied.")
else:
    print("No discount available.")

Here, the discount is applied because has_coupon is true, even though is_member is false.

Using not to reverse a condition

The not operator reverses a Boolean expression. It turns True into False and False into True.

is_logged_in = False
if not is_logged_in:
    print("Please log in to continue.")
else:
    print("Welcome back.")

not is often clearer when the variable name already describes a state. In this example, not is_logged_in reads naturally as “if the user is not logged in.”

A realistic decision: checking whether an order can ship

A warehouse system might need to check several facts before allowing an order to ship. The order should ship only if the item is in stock, the address is verified, and the payment has been approved.

in_stock = True
address_verified = True
payment_approved = False
if in_stock and address_verified and payment_approved:
    print("Order is ready to ship.")
else:
    print("Order cannot ship yet.")

This single condition represents a business rule. If any required part is false, the program chooses the safer response and does not mark the order as ready.

Nested decisions for complex cases

Sometimes it is useful to place one if statement inside another. This is called nesting. Nested conditionals can make sense when a second decision should only be considered after the first decision passes.

account_active = True
purchase_total = 120
is_member = True
if account_active:
    if purchase_total >= 100 and is_member:
        print("Member reward applied.")
    else:
        print("No member reward for this purchase.")
else:
    print("Account is inactive.")

In this example, the reward rules are checked only when the account is active. This structure makes the main requirement visible before the program checks the more detailed condition.

However, nesting too deeply can make code harder to follow. When a condition can be written clearly on one line, a combined condition may be easier to read.

Ineffective approach Why it is harder to read Effective approach
if age >= 18:
    if has_ticket:
        print("Entry allowed.")		 The nested structure is unnecessary because both conditions are part of the same rule. if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Entry allowed.")
if not score >= 60: The meaning may take a moment to interpret. if score < 60: is usually clearer.

Debugging indentation and colon errors

Python expects a colon after each conditional header and an indented block underneath it. These two syntax rules are small but essential.

temperature = 18
if temperature < 20:
    print("Wear a jacket.")

The following version has two common errors: the colon is missing, and the line that should belong to the if block is not indented.

temperature = 18
if temperature < 20
print("Wear a jacket.")

When debugging conditionals, check the structure before changing the logic. Ask whether every if and elif has a condition, whether every if, elif, and else ends with a colon, and whether the controlled statements are indented consistently.

Activity: write an access rule

Write a program that decides whether a user can access a premium article. Create these variables:

  • is_logged_in, storing either True or False.
  • has_subscription, storing either True or False.
  • free_articles_remaining, storing a number.

The user should be allowed access if they are logged in and either have a subscription or have at least one free article remaining. Print "Access granted" or "Access denied". After writing your first version, test it with different combinations of values and identify which part of the condition controls each result.

is_logged_in = True
has_subscription = False
free_articles_remaining = 2
if is_logged_in and (has_subscription or free_articles_remaining > 0):
    print("Access granted")
else:
    print("Access denied")

The parentheses make the intended grouping clear: the user must be logged in, and then one of the two access options must be true.

This chapter has shown how Python programs make decisions with if, elif, and else, how comparison operators produce true-or-false conditions, how logical operators combine multiple rules, how nested conditionals can represent layered decisions, and how careful use of colons and indentation keeps conditional code valid and readable.

    grade = "Needs improvement"

A realistic decision: choosing a shipping message
Online stores often show different messages depending on the value of an order. The program below uses a variable and several conditions to choose a helpful message.

order_total = 72.50
if order_total >= 100:
    message = "You qualify for free express shipping."
elif order_total >= 50:
    message = "You qualify for free standard shipping."
else:
    message = "Shipping costs will be added at checkout."
print(message)

Ineffective approach Why it causes problems Effective approach

elif score >= 90		 The 90 case is never reached because scores of 90 or higher already match score >= 70. Check the most specific or highest range first: if score >= 90, then elif score >= 70.

Common mistakes with basic conditionals

• Using = instead of == when comparing values.
  • Forgetting the colon after if, elif, or else.
  • Indenting inconsistently, which changes which lines belong to the conditional block.
  • Putting conditions in an order that makes later cases unreachable.
  • Using separate if statements when only one branch should run.
Activity: classify an account balance
Create a variable named balance and write a conditional chain that prints one of three messages:

• "Overdrawn" if the balance is less than 0.
  • "Low balance" if the balance is from 0 up to, but not including, 100.
  • "Balance is healthy" if the balance is 100 or more.
Test your code with at least three different values, such as -15, 50, and 200. After each test, check whether the output matches the condition you intended.

This condition requires both rules to pass: the person must be at least 18 and must have a ticket. If either part is false, the entire condition is false.
Because has_ticket already stores a Boolean value, the comparison can be written more directly:

age = 20
has_ticket = True
if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Entry allowed.")
else:
    print("Entry denied.")

The or operator produces True when at least one side is true. This is useful for alternative ways to qualify for the same outcome.

has_coupon = True

else:
    print("No discount available.")
Here, the discount is applied because has_coupon is true, even though is_member is false.

The not operator reverses a Boolean expression. It turns True into False and False into True.

    print("Please log in to continue.")
else:
    print("Welcome back.")

address_verified = True

    print("Entry allowed.")

if temperature < 20
print("Wear a jacket.")

• is_logged_in, storing either True or False.
  • has_subscription, storing either True or False.
  • free_articles_remaining, storing a number.

else:
    print("Access denied")

chapter.title: Repeating tasks with loops
chapter.html:
Iterating with for loops

A for loop is useful when your program needs to process a known sequence of values. Instead of writing the same instruction many times, you write the instruction once and let Python repeat it for each item. This works especially well with values you can count through, such as a range of numbers, or collections you can visit one item at a time, such as strings and lists.

The loop variable temporarily stores the current item during each repetition. In the example below, day takes each value from the list, one after another:

week_temperatures = [72, 75, 71, 69, 74]
for temperature in week_temperatures:
    print("Recorded temperature:", temperature)

The indented line belongs to the loop, so it runs once for each value in week_temperatures. This continues the same indentation pattern you have already used with if, elif, and else: the colon introduces a block, and indentation shows which statements are controlled by that structure.

Looping through a range of numbers

When you need a sequence of numbers, range() creates one for the loop to use. The most common form is range(stop), which starts at 0 and stops before the given number:

for number in range(5):
    print(number)

This prints 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. The stop value is not included. This is a common source of off-by-one mistakes, especially when you expect range(5) to include 5.

You can also use range(start, stop) to choose where counting begins:

for floor in range(1, 6):
    print("Checking floor", floor)

This is more natural when modeling a real-world task such as checking floors 1 through 5 in a building. To control how much the number changes each time, use range(start, stop, step):

for minute in range(0, 31, 5):
    print("Backup progress check at minute", minute)

This prints progress checks at minutes 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30. The step can also be negative when counting down:

for seconds in range(10, 0, -1):
    print(seconds)
print("Launch!")

Looping through strings and lists

A for loop can visit each character in a string. This is useful for tasks such as counting symbols, checking formatting, or analyzing text:

product_code = "A7B9"
for character in product_code:
    print("Checking:", character)

Lists are often used when you have several related values to process. For example, an online store might apply the same rule to each item price:

prices = [19.99, 5.50, 12.00, 3.75]
total = 0
for price in prices:
    total = total + price
print("Cart total:", total)

Each repetition adds the current price to total. This pattern is called accumulation: the program keeps a running result as the loop works through the data.

Ineffective and effective repetition

Approach Example Why it matters
Ineffective print(prices[0])
print(prices[1])
print(prices[2])		 This only works if the list length never changes. It is repetitive and easy to break.
Effective for price in prices:
    print(price)		 This works for short lists, long lists, and lists whose length changes.

The effective version describes the pattern instead of manually naming every position. This makes your code shorter and more flexible.

Common pitfalls with for loops

  • Forgetting that range() stops before the stop value, such as expecting range(1, 5) to include 5.
  • Using a loop variable outside the loop as if it contains every value, when it only contains one value at a time.
  • Indenting too much or too little, which changes whether a statement repeats or runs once after the loop.
  • Trying to add numbers stored as strings without converting them first, which can produce concatenation instead of arithmetic.

Practice with for loops

Create a list named daily_steps with five step counts. Use a for loop to calculate the total number of steps. Then print the total. After that, adjust your program to count how many days had at least 10000 steps.

daily_steps = [8500, 12000, 9400, 15000, 10200]
total_steps = 0
active_days = 0
for steps in daily_steps:
    total_steps = total_steps + steps
    if steps >= 10000:
        active_days = active_days + 1
print("Total steps:", total_steps)
print("Days with at least 10000 steps:", active_days)

Controlling loops with while

A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains true. It is useful when you do not know in advance exactly how many repetitions are needed. Instead of looping through a fixed sequence, the loop keeps checking a condition before each repetition.

battery_level = 5
while battery_level > 0:
    print("Battery level:", battery_level)
    battery_level = battery_level - 1
print("Battery empty")

Here, the loop continues while battery_level > 0. The update battery_level = battery_level - 1 is essential because it moves the program closer to making the condition false. Without that update, the condition would stay true and the loop would not stop on its own.

Using while when the stopping point depends on a condition

Imagine a simple security system that allows a limited number of passcode attempts. The loop should continue while attempts remain and the correct code has not been entered. Because this example does not use user input yet, it simulates attempts with a list:

correct_code = "4821"
attempts = ["1111", "2222", "4821"]
attempt_index = 0
unlocked = False
while attempt_index < len(attempts) and unlocked == False:
    current_attempt = attempts[attempt_index]
    if current_attempt == correct_code:
        unlocked = True
        print("Access granted")
    else:
        print("Incorrect code")
    attempt_index = attempt_index + 1

This loop is controlled by two conditions: there must be another attempt available, and the system must still be locked. The variable attempt_index is updated each time so the loop can move through the list and eventually stop.

Avoiding infinite loops

An infinite loop happens when the loop condition never becomes false. Sometimes infinite loops are used intentionally in advanced programs, but for beginner programs they are usually a sign that something is missing.

Version Code Result
Ineffective count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count)		 count never changes, so the condition stays true.
Effective count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1		 count increases until the condition becomes false.

When writing a while loop, ask: what value controls the condition, and where does that value change? If you cannot answer both questions, the loop may not stop correctly.

Using break and continue

The break statement exits a loop early. This is useful when the loop has found what it needs and continuing would waste work or produce unwanted output.

items = ["notebook", "pen", "charger", "water bottle"]
target = "charger"
for item in items:
    if item == target:
        print("Found:", item)
        break
    print("Checked:", item)

When item is "charger", the loop prints that it was found and stops immediately. The remaining items are not checked.

The continue statement skips the rest of the current repetition and moves to the next one. This is helpful when some values should be ignored but the loop itself should keep running.

scores = [88, -1, 92, 75, -1, 84]
total = 0
valid_scores = 0
for score in scores:
    if score == -1:
        continue
    total = total + score
    valid_scores = valid_scores + 1
print("Total of valid scores:", total)
print("Number of valid scores:", valid_scores)

In this example, -1 represents a missing score. The loop skips those values and only adds real scores to the total.

Common pitfalls with while loops

  • Forgetting to update the variable used in the loop condition.
  • Writing a condition that starts false, causing the loop body to never run.
  • Using break too early, which can stop the loop before important work is finished.
  • Using continue before an update statement in a while loop, which can accidentally create an infinite loop.
count = 0
while count < 5:
    count = count + 1
    if count == 3:
        continue
    print(count)

In this safer version, count is updated before continue can skip the rest of the loop body. The program avoids getting stuck when count reaches 3.

Practice with while loops

Write a countdown that starts at 10 and stops at 1. Skip printing 5, and stop the loop early if the number reaches 2. Before running your code, predict which numbers will appear.

countdown = 10
while countdown > 0:
    if countdown == 5:
        countdown = countdown - 1
        continue
    if countdown == 2:
        break
    print(countdown)
    countdown = countdown - 1

This chapter taught how to repeat work with for loops over ranges, strings, and lists; how to use range() with start, stop, and step values; how to build running totals and counts; how to control repetition with while conditions; how to prevent infinite loops by updating loop variables; and how break and continue change the normal flow of a loop.

chapter.title: Defining and using functions
chapter.html:
Creating your own functions

In earlier programs, you used loops to avoid writing the same repeated action many times. Functions solve a related problem at a higher level: they let you give a name to a complete task, then run that task whenever your program needs it. A function can receive information, process it, and send a result back to the rest of the program.

A Python function starts with def, followed by the function name, parentheses, and a colon. The indented lines underneath form the function body. The body does not run when Python first reads the function definition; it runs only when the function is called.

def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    total = price * quantity
    return total
book_total = calculate_total(12.99, 3)
print(book_total)

In this example, price and quantity are parameters. They act like named placeholders inside the function. The values 12.99 and 3 are arguments passed into the function call. The return statement sends the calculated value back so it can be stored, printed, compared, or used in another calculation.

Arguments by position and keyword

When you call a function, Python can match arguments to parameters by position. The first argument goes into the first parameter, the second argument goes into the second parameter, and so on.

def format_score(name, points):
    return name + ": " + str(points) + " points"
message = format_score("Maya", 42)
print(message)

You can also use keyword arguments, which explicitly name the parameter receiving each value. This is especially useful when a function has several parameters or when the values might be easy to confuse.

message = format_score(points=42, name="Maya")
print(message)

Both calls produce the same result, but the keyword version makes the meaning of each argument clearer. For beginner programs, positional arguments are common for short functions, while keyword arguments are helpful when readability matters more than brevity.

Returning values instead of only printing

A common early habit is to put print() inside every function. Printing is useful when you want to display something, but returning a value makes the function more flexible. A returned value can be reused by other parts of the program.

Ineffective approach More effective approach

The function prints the result immediately, so the program cannot easily reuse the calculated value.

The function returns the result, allowing the caller to decide what to do with it.

 
def show_discounted_price(price):
    discount = price * 0.10
    final_price = price - discount
    print(final_price)
show_discounted_price(50)
def calculate_discounted_price(price):
    discount = price * 0.10
    final_price = price - discount
    return final_price
sale_price = calculate_discounted_price(50)
print("Sale price:", sale_price)
if sale_price < 45:
    print("Good deal")

The second version separates calculation from display. This design is useful in real programs such as checkout systems, grade calculators, budget trackers, and simple games because the same function result can support multiple decisions.

A realistic function example

Imagine a small delivery business that charges a base fee plus an extra cost per kilometer. A function can represent that business rule clearly.

def calculate_delivery_fee(distance_km):
    base_fee = 4.00
    cost_per_km = 1.25
    fee = base_fee + distance_km * cost_per_km
    return fee
short_trip = calculate_delivery_fee(3)
long_trip = calculate_delivery_fee(12)
print("Short trip fee:", short_trip)
print("Long trip fee:", long_trip)

This function makes the program easier to adjust. If the delivery company changes its base fee, you update the rule in one place instead of searching through the whole program for repeated calculations.

Common mistakes when writing functions

  • Forgetting to call the function: defining a function stores the instructions, but the body runs only when the function name is followed by parentheses.

  • Mixing up parameter order: with positional arguments, format_score("Maya", 42) is different from format_score(42, "Maya").

  • Expecting print() to return a useful value: print() displays output but does not send the displayed text back as a reusable result.

  • Forgetting return: if a function does not return a value, Python gives back None.

Practice task

Write a function named calculate_average that accepts three numbers and returns their average. Call it at least twice with different arguments. Then use one returned average in an if statement to print whether the average is at least 70.

Understanding variable scope and function design

Functions create boundaries in your program. A variable made inside a function is local to that function, which means it belongs to that function body. A variable made outside functions is global, which means it exists in the wider script. Understanding this boundary helps prevent confusing bugs, especially as programs grow beyond a few lines.

def calculate_tax(price):
    tax_rate = 0.08
    tax = price * tax_rate
    return tax
item_tax = calculate_tax(100)
print(item_tax)

Here, tax_rate and tax are local variables. They are created while calculate_tax is running and are not meant to be used directly outside the function. The program outside the function receives only what the function returns.

Local and global variables in practice

Local variables are usually safer because they keep a function self-contained. A self-contained function is easier to test and reuse because it depends mainly on its parameters, not on hidden values elsewhere in the program.

tax_rate = 0.08
def calculate_tax(price):
    return price * tax_rate
print(calculate_tax(100))

This code works, but the function depends on the global variable tax_rate. If another part of the program changes tax_rate, the function’s behavior changes too. That can be useful in some advanced designs, but for beginner programs it often makes code harder to understand.

def calculate_tax(price, tax_rate):
    return price * tax_rate
print(calculate_tax(100, 0.08))

This version is more explicit. The function receives the tax rate it needs, so the caller can clearly see what information affects the result.

Default parameter values

A default parameter value lets a function use a standard value when the caller does not provide one. This is helpful when most calls use the same value, but you still want the option to customize it.

def calculate_tax(price, tax_rate=0.08):
    return price * tax_rate
standard_tax = calculate_tax(100)
special_tax = calculate_tax(100, tax_rate=0.05)
print(standard_tax)
print(special_tax)

Interacting with the user

Turning keyboard input into usable program data

Interactive programs pause, ask the user for information, and then continue based on the answer. In Python, input() reads text typed from the keyboard. Even if the user types 42, Python receives it as a string, so calculation requires an explicit conversion before arithmetic.

name = input("What is your name? ")
age_text = input("How old are you? ")
age = int(age_text)
age_next_year = age + 1
print(f"Hello, {name}. Next year, you will be {age_next_year}.")

The prompt inside input() should make the expected answer clear. A vague prompt such as input("Enter value: ") forces the user to guess. A specific prompt such as input("Enter the price before tax: ") gives the program better data and makes errors less likely.

Formatting output for clarity

The print() function is most useful when the output explains the result, not just displays a raw value. F-strings let you place variables directly inside a message, which keeps output readable and connected to the calculation.

item = input("Item name: ")
price = float(input("Price: "))
tax_rate = 0.08
total = price + (price * tax_rate)
print(f"The total price for {item} is ${total:.2f}.")

This kind of output is common in real programs: receipt systems, booking tools, budget calculators, grade trackers, and inventory scripts all collect user input, process it, and present a result that a person can understand quickly.

Ineffective and effective interaction patterns

Ineffective approach Effective approach
input("Number: ") with no context input("Enter the number of tickets: ") gives a clear expectation
Calculating with the original input string Convert with int() or float() before arithmetic
print(total) only print(f"Your total is ${total:.2f}.") explains the result

Common pitfalls with input and output

  • Forgetting that input() returns a string, then trying to add it to a number.
  • Using int() when decimal values are valid, such as prices or measurements.
  • Writing prompts that do not tell the user what kind of value to enter.
  • Printing results without labels, which makes output hard to interpret.

Activity: make a simple tip calculator

Create a short program that asks for a meal cost and a tip percentage. Convert both inputs to numbers, calculate the tip amount and final total, then print both values using f-strings with two decimal places. After writing it, test it with a whole-number price and a decimal price.

Final project: a simple calculator

Designing the calculator before coding

A small calculator is a useful final project because it combines input, conversion, conditionals, functions, and output. The program should ask for two numbers and one operator, then choose the correct calculation. Since functions help separate responsibilities, each operation can be placed in its own function or one function can coordinate the calculation.

The basic design is:

  1. Ask the user for the first number.
  2. Ask the user for an operator: +, -, *, or /.
  3. Ask the user for the second number.
  4. Convert the number inputs to float values.
  5. Use conditionals to select the correct operation.
  6. Handle invalid numbers, unknown operators, and division by zero.
  7. Print a clear result.

Handling invalid input with try and except

User input is unpredictable. A person might type ten instead of 10, or choose an operator the program does not support. Python can respond to certain runtime problems using try and except. Code inside try is attempted; if a matching error occurs, the except block runs instead of crashing the program.

try:
    number = float(input("Enter a number: "))
    print(f"You entered {number}.")
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a valid number.")

This is especially important in interactive programs because the user sees a helpful message instead of a technical traceback.

A complete calculator implementation

def calculate(first_number, operator, second_number):
    if operator == "+":
        return first_number + second_number
    elif operator == "-":
        return first_number - second_number
    elif operator == "*":
        return first_number * second_number
    elif operator == "/":
        if second_number == 0:
            return "Cannot divide by zero."
        return first_number / second_number
    else:
        return "Invalid operator."
try:
    first = float(input("Enter the first number: "))
    operator = input("Enter an operator (+, -, *, /): ")
    second = float(input("Enter the second number: "))
    result = calculate(first, operator, second)
    if isinstance(result, str):
        print(result)
    else:
        print(f"{first} {operator} {second} = {result:.2f}")
except ValueError:
    print("Invalid number. Please enter numeric values only.")

This version keeps the calculation logic inside calculate(), while the input and output stay in the main part of the program. That separation makes the code easier to test and adjust. For example, you could test calculate(8, "*", 3) without typing anything into the keyboard.

Ineffective and effective calculator structure

Ineffective approach Effective approach
Put all input, decisions, arithmetic, and printing into one long block Use a function for the calculation and keep interaction code separate
Assume every input can be converted successfully Use try and except ValueError around numeric conversion
Allow division by zero to crash or produce confusing behavior Check for second_number == 0 before division
Print only the result number Print the full expression and formatted answer

Common pitfalls in the project

  • Checking for division by zero after performing the division, when the error has already happened.
  • Comparing the operator to words like "plus" when the prompt asks for symbols like "+".
  • Returning some results as numbers and some as strings without checking before formatting.
  • Using int() and accidentally rejecting valid decimal calculations such as 7.5 / 2.

Activity: improve the calculator

Run the calculator several times using normal and unusual inputs. Test 10 / 2, 10 / 0, 4 * 2.5, an invalid operator such as %, and a non-number such as five. Then add one improvement: either allow the user to type another calculation in a loop, or add exponentiation using the ** operator.

chapter.title: Getting started with Python
chapter.html:
What is Python and why learn it?

Python is a general-purpose programming language, which means it can be used to build many different kinds of software rather than being limited to one narrow task. It was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. One of Python’s main design goals is readability: Python code is meant to look close to plain English compared with many other programming languages.

A programming language lets you give precise instructions to a computer. Python is especially popular because it works well for beginners while also being powerful enough for professional projects. It is used in web development, data science, automation, education, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, game scripting, and scientific computing.

Where Python is used in real work

Python often appears in situations where people need to process information, automate repeated actions, or build software quickly. For example, a small business might use Python to rename hundreds of invoice files, extract totals from spreadsheets, or send automatic email reminders. A data analyst might use Python to clean survey results and create charts. A web developer might use Python to build the server side of a website, such as handling user accounts or storing form submissions.

Domain Example use Why Python fits
Automation Rename files, organize folders, generate reports Python can interact with files, dates, text, and operating system tools
Data science Analyze sales, survey, or experiment data Python has strong libraries for tables, statistics, and visualization
Web development Create websites and web APIs Python frameworks help developers build reliable server-side applications
Education Learn programming fundamentals Python syntax is readable and beginner-friendly

Why Python is beginner-friendly

Python is not “easy” because computers are easy; programming still requires careful thinking. Python is beginner-friendly because it removes some unnecessary complexity from the first learning experience. Its syntax is relatively clean, and common operations can often be written in a small number of lines.

For example, this Python program displays a message:

print("Hello, Python!")

The instruction print() tells Python to display output. The text inside quotation marks is a string, which means a piece of text data. You do not need to understand every detail yet. For now, notice that the code is readable: it looks like a direct instruction.

Less effective and more effective ways to start

A less effective approach is to begin by memorizing many commands without understanding what they do. This can make programming feel like copying magic phrases. A more effective approach is to connect each line of code to a simple question: What instruction am I giving? What information does it use? What result should I expect?

Less effective approach

More effective approach

Copying code without running it

Running code and observing the exact output

Trying to learn every Python feature at once

Learning a small concept, then testing it with examples

Ignoring error messages

Reading error messages as clues about what Python could not understand

Typing large programs immediately

Starting with short programs that are easy to inspect

Setting up Python

To run Python programs, your computer needs a Python interpreter. An interpreter is a program that reads your Python code and carries out the instructions. You can install Python from the official Python website at https://www.python.org/downloads/.

Windows

  1. Download the latest stable Python installer from the official website.

  1. Run the installer.

  2. On the first installer screen, select Add python.exe to PATH if the option appears.

  3. Choose the standard installation option.

  4. Open Command Prompt or PowerShell and verify the installation.

py --version

macOS

  1. Download the macOS installer from the official Python website, or use a trusted package manager if you already know one.

  2. Run the installer and follow the prompts.

  3. Open Terminal and verify the installation.

python3 --version

Linux

Many Linux systems already include Python. Open a terminal and check the installed version:

python3 --version

If Python is not installed, use your distribution’s package manager. For example, on Debian-based systems such as Ubuntu, you may use:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3

Common setup pitfalls

  • Using the wrong command: On Windows, py often works. On macOS and Linux, python3 is commonly used.
  • Forgetting PATH on Windows: If the command is not recognized, Python may be installed but not available from the command line.
  • Installing from an unofficial source: Prefer the official Python website or your operating system’s trusted package manager.
  • Confusing Python with a code editor: Python runs code. A code editor helps you write code. They are related, but not the same thing.

Short activity: connect Python to a real task

Choose one repeated computer task from your daily life, schoolwork, or job. Write one or two sentences describing how Python might help. For example: “I often download files with messy names. Python could rename them using a consistent date and category format.” Then verify your Python installation by running the version command for your operating system.

Writing your first Python program

There are two common ways to begin using Python: the interactive shell and script

files. The interactive shell is useful for quick experiments because you type one instruction and see the result immediately. A script file is better for saving a program so you can run it again later.

Using the interactive shell

Open a terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell. Start Python with the command that matches your system. On Windows, this is often:

py

On macOS or Linux, this is often:

python3

When the Python prompt appears, it usually looks like this:

>>>

You can use the shell like a calculator:

>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> 10 * 4
40
>>> print("Python is running")
Python is running

The shell is useful because it gives immediate feedback. If you are unsure what a small expression does, you can test it quickly. To leave the shell, you can usually type exit() and press Enter.

>>> exit()

Creating a script file

A script is a saved file containing Python instructions. Create a new file in a plain-text code editor and name it hello.py. The .py extension tells you and your tools that the file contains Python code.

Type this code into the file:

print("Hello, Python!")
print("This is my first script.")

Save the file. Then open a terminal in the same folder as the file and run it. On Windows, use:

py hello.py

On macOS or Linux, use:

python3 hello.py

You should see:

Hello, Python!
This is my first script.

Understanding input, processing, and output

A program can be understood as a sequence that receives or uses information, processes it, and produces a result. This is often described as input, processing, output.

  • Input: The information a program starts with. This might come from a user, a file, a sensor, a website, or values written in the program.
  • Processing: The steps the program performs, such as calculating, comparing, organizing, or formatting information.
  • Output: The result the program produces, such as printed text, a saved file, a chart, or an action.

In the first script, the input is the text written inside the code, the processing is Python carrying out the print() instructions, and the output is the displayed text.

Here is a slightly more realistic example from a small shop preparing a receipt message:

print("Receipt")
print("Item: notebook")
print("Price: $4.50")
print("Thank you for your purchase!")

This is still simple, but it already shows a useful pattern: a program can turn stored information into clear output. Later, programs can become more flexible by using information that changes, but the basic structure remains the same: information goes in, instructions are applied, and a result comes out.

A less effective first program tries to do too many things at once: calculations, user interaction, file saving, and complex formatting all in one attempt. Storing data with variables

In your first Python programs, you printed fixed messages. Variables let a program remember information while it runs, so the program can process values instead of only displaying text that never changes. A variable is a name that refers to a value. You create one with an assignment statement, using the equals sign =.

student_name = "Maya"
lesson_count = 2
print(student_name)
print(lesson_count)

Using if statements to make choices

Programs become more useful when they can choose between different actions. An if statement tells Python to run a block of code only when a condition is true. A condition is an expression that produces either True or False, often by comparing values stored in variables.

temperature = 32
if temperature >= 30:
    print("It is a hot day.")

The line ending with a colon starts the decision. The indented line below it belongs to the if block. Python uses indentation to understand which statements are controlled by the decision.

How comparisons create decisions

Comparison operators let your program ask precise questions about values. The result of each comparison is a Boolean value: True or False.

Operator Meaning Example Result if score = 80
== Equal to score == 80 True
!= Not equal to score != 80 False
< Less than score < 80 False
> Greater than score > 80 False
<= Less than or equal to score <= 80 True
>= Greater than or equal to score >= 80 True

A common beginner mistake is confusing = and ==. A single = assigns a value to a variable. A double == compares two values.

score = 80      # assignment
score == 80     # comparison

Adding alternatives with else and elif

An if statement handles one possible path. An else block handles the opposite case. This is useful when a program must choose between two outcomes.

account_balance = 45
purchase_total = 30
if account_balance >= purchase_total:
    print("Purchase approved.")
else:
    print("Not enough funds.")

For more than two possibilities, use elif, which means “else if.” Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is true. After that, the rest of the chain is skipped.

score = 86
if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
else:
    grade = "Needs improvement"
print(grade)

The order matters. In the example above, score >= 80 must come before score >= 70. If broader conditions are placed too early, more specific conditions may never run.

A realistic decision: choosing a shipping message

Online stores often show different messages depending on the value of an order. The program below uses a variable and several conditions to choose a helpful message.

order_total = 72.50
if order_total >= 100:
    message = "You qualify for free express shipping."
elif order_total >= 50:
    message = "You qualify for free standard shipping."
else:
    message = "Shipping costs will be added at checkout."
print(message)

This is more flexible than writing separate one-off print statements because the program chooses the message based on the current value of order_total. If the value changes, the decision changes with it.

Ineffective and effective condition chains

Ineffective approach Why it causes problems Effective approach
if score >= 70
elif score >= 90		 The 90 case is never reached because scores of 90 or higher already match score >= 70. Check the most specific or highest range first: if score >= 90, then elif score >= 70.
Using several separate if statements for one exclusive choice More than one block might run when only one result should be selected. Use an if, elif, else chain when the choices are mutually exclusive.
Writing vague conditions such as if total before understanding the intended test The code may technically run but be hard to read or reason about. Write explicit comparisons such as if total >= 50 when checking a threshold.

Common mistakes with basic conditionals

  • Using = instead of == when comparing values.
  • Forgetting the colon after if, elif, or else.
  • Indenting inconsistently, which changes which lines belong to the conditional block.
  • Putting conditions in an order that makes later cases unreachable.
  • Using separate if statements when only one branch should run.

Activity: classify an account balance

Create a variable named balance and write a conditional chain that prints one of three messages:

  • "Overdrawn" if the balance is less than 0.
  • "Low balance" if the balance is from 0 up to, but not including, 100.
  • "Balance is healthy" if the balance is 100 or more.

Test your code with at least three different values, such as -15, 50, and 200. After each test, check whether the output matches the condition you intended.

Combining conditions with logical operators

Many real decisions depend on more than one condition. Python provides logical operators that combine Boolean expressions: and, or, and not. These operators help you express rules such as “the user must be old enough and have permission” or “apply a discount if the customer is a member or has a coupon.”

Using and when all conditions must be true

The and operator produces True only when both sides are true.

age = 20
has_ticket = True
if age >= 18 and has_ticket == True:
    print("Entry allowed.")
else:
    print("Entry denied.")

This condition requires both rules to pass: the person must be at least 18 and must have a ticket. If either part is false, the entire condition is false.

Because has_ticket already stores a Boolean value, the comparison can be written more directly:

age = 20
has_ticket = True
if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Entry allowed.")
else:
    print("Entry denied.")

Using or when at least one condition may be true

The or operator produces True when at least one side is true. This is useful for alternative ways to qualify for the same outcome.

is_member = False
has_coupon = True
if is_member or has_coupon:
    print("Discount applied.")
else:
    print("No discount available.")

Here, the discount is applied because has_coupon is true, even though is_member is false.

Using not to reverse a condition

The not operator reverses a Boolean expression. It turns True into False and False into True.

is_logged_in = False
if not is_logged_in:
    print("Please log in to continue.")
else:
    print("Welcome back.")

not is often clearer when the variable name already describes a state. In this example, not is_logged_in reads naturally as “if the user is not logged in.”

A warehouse system might need to check several facts before allowing an order to ship. The order should ship only if the item is in stock, the address is verified, and the payment has been approved.

address_verified = True
payment_approved = False
if in_stock and address_verified and payment_approved:
    print("Order is ready to ship.")
else:
    print("Order cannot ship yet.")

This single condition represents a business rule. If any required part is false, the program chooses the safer response and does not mark the order as ready.

Nested decisions for complex cases

Sometimes it is useful to place one if statement inside another. This is called nesting. Nested conditionals can make sense when a second decision should only be considered after the first decision passes.

account_active = True
purchase_total = 120
is_member = True
if account_active:
    if purchase_total >= 100 and is_member:
        print("Member reward applied.")
    else:
        print("No member reward for this purchase.")
else:
    print("Account is inactive.")

In this example, the reward rules are checked only when the account is active. This structure makes the main requirement visible before the program checks the more detailed condition.

However, nesting too deeply can make code harder to follow. When a condition can be written clearly on one line, a combined condition may be easier to read.

Ineffective approach Why it is harder to read Effective approach
if age >= 18:
    if has_ticket:
        print("Entry allowed.")		 The nested structure is unnecessary because both conditions are part of the same rule. if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Entry allowed.")
if not score >= 60: The meaning may take a moment to interpret. if score < 60: is usually clearer.

Debugging indentation and colon errors

Python expects a colon after each conditional header and an indented block underneath it. These two syntax rules are small but essential.

temperature = 18
if temperature < 20:
    print("Wear a jacket.")

The following version has two common errors: the colon is missing, and the line that should belong to the if block is not indented.

temperature = 18
if temperature < 20
print("Wear a jacket.")

When debugging conditionals, check the structure before changing the logic. Ask whether every if and elif has a condition, whether every if, elif, and else ends with a colon, and whether the controlled statements are indented consistently.

Write a program that decides whether a user can access a premium article. Create these variables:

  • is_logged_in, storing either True or False.
  • has_subscription, storing either True or False.
  • free_articles_remaining, storing a number.

The user should be allowed access if they are logged in and either have a subscription or have at least one free article remaining. Print "Access granted" or "Access denied". After writing your first version, test it with different combinations of values and identify which part of the condition controls each result.

is_logged_in = True
has_subscription = False
free_articles_remaining = 2
if is_logged_in and (has_subscription or free_articles_remaining > 0):
    print("Access granted")
else:
    print("Access denied")

The parentheses make the intended grouping clear: the user must be logged in, and then one of the two access options must be true.
